conclusion: Senra rereads Henry Singleton as the CEO Buffett said most bosses are unprepared to be: a capital allocator, not a Carnegie Hall musician suddenly chairing the Fed. Teledyne (captions: Teladine) compounded 20.4% a year from 1963 to 1990 — $1 became $180. Munger called the returns utterly ridiculous. Singleton bought 130 companies in 1961–69 with pricey conglomerate stock, then flipped to aggressive buybacks when the stock was cheap, eventually owning over 90%. No dividends, cash flow over earnings, decentralized ops, never split the stock, the Sphinx to analysts. Insurance float was the largest book, the same tool Buffett used.
background: Methods tape on Singleton — MIT's first computer, WWII radar-evasion, 1950s aircraft guidance, then Teledyne. Conglomerates were the internet stocks of the 1960s. Senra's operator takeaway is capital allocation as the scarce CEO skill.
important_facts: Scoreboard: 20.4% annual compound 1963–1990; $1 → $180 when he stepped down. Munger: returns a mile higher than anyone else's, utterly ridiculous. Buffett: most CEOs rise through marketing/production/engineering/politics and then must allocate capital they have never practiced. Singleton gave most of his attention to deploying cash, not running plants. Avoided dividends, emphasized cash flow over reported earnings, never split the stock, refused the analyst circuit (the Sphinx).

Two regimes: 1961–69 he purchased 130 companies (aviation electronics, specialty metals, insurance). All but two were bought with Teledyne's high-PE 1960s paper — conglomerates were the era's internet stocks. After the multiple collapsed he inverted: 1972 he announced a tender because 'our stock is simply too cheap' and he could earn more buying shares than almost anything else. Buybacks were then uncommon and treated as a lack of internal projects. He kept tendering until he had over 90% of the shares.

Same toolkit as Buffett: both saw insurance float as investable capital and made insurance the largest, most important business. Decentralized operations; headquarters did capital allocation. Frugality stories (poker-parlor lunches, making the junior pick up the check) are the culture print. WWII and 1950s guidance work is the technical biography before the conglomerate — he was a world-class mathematician who programmed MIT's first computer and played chess blindfolded.

mental_model.name: Issue Dear / Buy Cheap × Float × Sphinx HQ
mental_model.components: Use expensive stock as currency when the multiple is silly (130 deals, 1961–69). When the stock is cheap, tender until you own the company (90%+). Treat insurance float as the real capital account. Decentralize operations so HQ only allocates. Ignore analysts. Never split, skip the dividend, report cash. Most CEOs were promoted for a different sport — do not copy their allocation.
mental_model.application: TDY is the living remnant of the machine, not a 1960s replay. BRK.B is the parallel float/allocation story Senra cites. Fade CEOs who only run operations and outsource the balance sheet. A buyback is a project when the stock is the cheapest asset in the room. Do not pay conglomerate-era PE for a roll-up that cannot invert into repurchase.

key_insights.question: What did Buffett say most CEOs lack?
key_insights.answer: Capital allocation. They were hired for a plant skill and then named Fed chair.

key_insights.question: When do you issue vs tender?
key_insights.answer: 130 deals on high-PE paper, then 1972-on tenders because the stock was too cheap. He ended above 90%.

key_insights.question: Why insurance?
key_insights.answer: Same as Buffett: invest the float. Insurance became the largest business at both firms.
